posts.why: Opens with a number, your strongest pattern.
posts.text:
Most founders I talk to think they have 14 months of runway.

They have 9.

The gap comes from three things they leave out:

1. Annual contracts paid upfront. That cash is already spent on the months you owe the customer.
2. Hiring plans. Every open role in the plan is a cost from the start date, plus 3 months of ramp.
3. Payment terms. Net 60 customers fund you two months late.

Run the number again with all three in.

If it drops below 12 months, start the raise conversation now. Six months before you need it is the earliest that feels calm.

What number did you get?

posts.why: Story openings sit second in your peer set.
posts.text:
Last quarter a founder sent me his board deck at 11pm the night before the meeting.

42 slides.

We cut it to 9.

Here is what stayed:

- Cash and runway on slide 1
- The one metric the board cares about this quarter
- What changed since last time, in three lines
- The decision you need from them

The meeting ran 40 minutes shorter. The board approved the hire.

Your board reads slide 1 closely and skims the rest. Put the decision there.

posts.why: Number-led opening with a simple chart image.
posts.text:
A 2% monthly churn rate sounds small.

Over a year it removes about 22% of your customers.

That is why I treat churn as a cash flow line, and I put it next to burn in every model I build.

The chart shows what 1%, 2% and 3% monthly churn do to the same starting revenue over 12 months.

Which line is closest to yours?

posts.topic: Five numbers for your Monday review
posts.text:
Every Monday I check five numbers with each founder I work with.

It takes 15 minutes. It replaces a monthly panic.

The five are in the carousel. Steal the list and make it your own.

posts.topic: When to hire your first finance person
posts.why: Answers the question buyers asked under your posts.
posts.text:
Founders ask me this every week: when should I hire my first finance person?

My rule of thumb:

Under $1M ARR, a good bookkeeper plus a few hours of fractional help.
Between $1M and $5M, a fractional CFO for planning and the board.
Past $5M or a Series B, a full-time finance lead.

The trigger is usually the first board that asks a question nobody can answer by Friday.

Where are you on this ladder?

posts.topic: Discounts that cost you a year
posts.text:
A 20% discount on a $30k contract costs you $6k.

It also resets the price your customer remembers for the renewal.

Three things I ask founders to try first:

1. Trade the discount for a longer term.
2. Trade it for upfront payment.
3. Trade it for a case study.

You keep the price. You get something back.

The simplest finance tool I give founders is a cash flow calendar.

One row per week. Money in, money out, balance.

The carousel walks through how to build it in 20 minutes.

Comment CALENDAR and I will send you the template.

posts.why: Story-led, built from a real meeting type.
posts.text:
I sat in on 6 investor meetings with founders this year.

The first finance question was the same every time:

"How long does your cash last?"

Two founders answered in one sentence. Both got second meetings.

Know your runway to the month. Say it before they ask.

Gross margin is what you keep from each dollar after the costs of serving that customer.

For most SaaS companies, healthy sits between 70% and 80%.

If yours is lower, look at hosting, support and onboarding first.

The image shows where each of those costs usually sits.

posts.why: Seasonal and practical, a strong save driver.
posts.text:
Q4 planning checklist for SaaS founders:

- Update runway with real Q3 numbers
- Set next year's hiring plan by month
- Review pricing before renewals land
- Book your board date for January now
- Pick the one metric you will report every month

Five items. One afternoon.

Which one is still open for you?
